steps.heading: The mechanics of addition and subtraction
paragraphs: Addition is one of those skills you want to be able to do without thinking. Every later topic — algebra, percentages, ratio — leans on it, so fluency here pays off everywhere.
Work in columns, keep place value lined up, and check with the inverse operation: if 22 × 6 = 132, then 132 ÷ 6 = 22. That inverse check catches most slips instantly.
Estimate first with rounded numbers. If your estimate and your answer disagree wildly, one of them is wrong — and it is usually the written method, not the estimate.

steps.heading: Order of operations
paragraphs: BIDMAS tells you the order: Brackets, Indices, Division and Multiplication (left to right), Addition and Subtraction (left to right).
So 3 + 2 × 6 is 3 + 12 = 15 — the multiplication happens first. Writing the working in the BIDMAS order is what examiners want to see.
The trap is doing left-to-right blindly. Multiplication and division have equal priority, and so do addition and subtraction — ties are broken left to right only.

steps.heading: Factors, multiples, primes
paragraphs: A factor of 36 divides it exactly; a multiple of 36 is 36 times something. Factors come in pairs — for 36 there are 9 of them: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36.
A prime has exactly two factors. To test if p is prime, only try primes up to √p — if nothing divides p by then, nothing ever will.
Factor pairs are how product-and-sum puzzles get solved: you want two numbers that multiply to one target and add to another.

steps.heading: Using place value
paragraphs: Multiplication finds the total in equal groups, and the answer is called the product. Division shares into equal groups, and the answer is called the quotient.
Place value tells you what each digit is worth. For example, 572 = 500 + 70 + 2, so the 5 means 500, the 7 means 70, and the 2 means 2.
This split is useful because big calculations become smaller, safer ones. The same idea works with decimals too, using tenths and hundredths.

steps.heading: Multiple Choice Question
steps.question: Which is the correct place value split of 572?

options.label: A
options.why: A is correct because 5 is in the hundreds column, 7 is in the tens column, and 2 is in the ones column. Common wrong C reads the tens digit as 7 ones, but a 7 in the tens column is worth 70, not 7. Hint: think hundreds, tens, ones.

steps.heading: Making it easier
paragraphs: Split numbers by place value before multiplying: 324 × 5 = (300 × 5) + (20 × 5) + (4 × 5) = 1500 + 100 + 20 = 1620.
For division, ask 'how many groups fit?'. 1620 ÷ 5 means how many 5s make 1620 — the same fact as 324 × 5 = 1620, read backwards.
This is why checking with the inverse operation is so powerful: one fact verifies the other for free.

steps.heading: Rounding: the digit after decides
paragraphs: To round to a place, look at the digit immediately after it. 7353 to the nearest 10: the ones digit decides — 5 or more rounds up, 4 or less rounds down.

steps.heading: Two signs at a time

Multiply and divide by the sign rules: same signs give a positive, different signs give a negative. (−13) × (−10) = +130 while (−13) × 10 = −130.

steps.heading: The angle facts that run the show
paragraphs: Four totals unlock nearly every diagram: angles on a straight line (180°), around a point (360°), in a triangle (180°), and vertically opposite angles are equal.
With parallel lines, spot the shapes: Z-shape → alternate angles equal; F-shape → corresponding angles equal; C or U shape → co-interior angles sum to 180°.
Examiners award the reason as well as the number. Write 'alternate angles are equal' next to the line of working and the mark is yours.

steps.heading: Area and perimeter: two different questions
paragraphs: Area measures the surface (squared units); perimeter measures the boundary (plain units). For a 8 by 8 rectangle: area = 8 × 8 = 64, perimeter = 2 × (8 + 8) = 32.
Compound shapes split into rectangles (or triangles) — do each area, then add. Perimeter means walking the whole outline once, no more, no less.
Keep units attached: cm for length, cm² for area, cm³ for volume. Wrong units cost a mark even when the number is right.

steps.heading: Counting outcomes
paragraphs: Probability compares favourable outcomes with all outcomes: P(event) = successful ÷ total. It lives between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain).
A die: P(even) = 3/6 = 1/2. Two events that cannot happen together are mutually exclusive, and their probabilities add.
P(not A) = 1 − P(A) is the single most useful line in the topic — examiners love 'at least one' questions built on it.

steps.heading: Percentages are fractions of 100

The hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle — always the longest. The two legs can go either way round in the formula.
The theorem only works when there is a right angle. No right angle → no Pythagoras (that is what the sine and cosine rules are for later).

steps.heading: Meet the quadratic
paragraphs: A quadratic has an x² term as its highest power. Its graph is a symmetrical curve (a parabola); solving it means finding where y = 0 — the roots.
Factorise when you can: x² + 7x + 12 = (x + 3)(x + 4), so x = −3 or x = 4. You need two numbers that multiply to 12 and add to 7.
When factorising will not play, use the formula x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a. It always works; the discriminant b² − 4ac even tells you how many roots to expect.

steps.heading: Meet the quadratic
paragraphs: A quadratic has an x² term as its highest power. Its graph is a symmetrical curve (a parabola); solving it means finding where y = 0 — the roots.
